newsitem.title: JORDAN: COMMON ARAB MARKET: new urgency, same old barriers.
newsitem.headline: COMMON ARAB MARKET: new urgency, same old barriers.

text.p: Arab economists had a distinct sense of deja-vu on Thursday when foreign ministers from Syria, Egypt and six oil-rich Gulf states announced they were setting up a common market.

The planned economic bloc of eight countries, expected to start life as a free-trade zone, is the latest attempt by Arab states to unify their economies since they declared a common Arab market in Cairo in 1964.
Progress since then has been negligible.

Economists say the near-collapse of Middle East peace talks and a growing trend in world trade towards economic blocs may have given the idea greater urgency, but many obstacles blocking Arab economic unity 33 years ago remain in force today.
Varying tariff regimes, currency controls and clumsy public sector domination of business still pose major barriers to integration.
So do the differing legal systems, taxation levels, travel and property rights and investment incentives.
Small surprise then that business between Arab states accounts for less than eight percent of all Arab trade.

"The common Arab market declared 30 years ago was not implemented because of objective reasons on the ground," said economist Fahd Fanek. "Those reasons are still there and...they will continue to prevent this new market."

The new bloc proposed at a ministerial meeting in the Mediterranean port of Latakia on Thursday groups eight countries with widely diverse economies. Two of them, Egypt and Syria, do not share a border with any of their proposed partners.
The six Gulf states are Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman and the United Arab Emirates.
Syria's 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) is estimated by the United Nations at $1,366 per person, less than one twelfth of oil-rich United Arab Emirates, at $17,272.

Even the Gulf Arab states, with largely similar economies, are still arguing over how to unify their tariffs 16 years after they formed the political and economic grouping known as the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) in 1981.
"The GCC countries, which are closely integrated, so far failed to have a common market between them. So how come they will open to Egypt and Syria when they can't open to each other?" Fanek asked.
"I don't give it much chance," he added.
But some analysts detected signs for optimism, saying pressure for integration could overcome differences in wealth and exports.

"They can be complementary," said Hazem Beblawi, an Egyptian banker who heads the U.N.'s Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia (ESCWA), which covers all eight countries of the new economic bloc.

Although Arabs merely paid lip service to the joint market in the past, there were new factors pushing them together, he said, including a shift towards private sector involvement in economies and a realisation that negotiations with economic blocs like the European Union would be easier as a group.

"They don't have much choice. They deal on a bilateral basis and they realise that they could do better," Beblawi told Reuters. Egypt has been engaged in protracted negotiations for years with the European Union over an association agreement.
The present poor state of Arab-Israeli relations was another incentive to close ranks economically, Beblawi said.
"The Arab states came to realise that one of the reasons for their weak positions is that the Israelis don't have an economic incentive to preserve the peace process," he said.
The great majority of Israel's trade is with industrialised nations rather than its Arab neighbours.
"A grouping of Arab economies would show Israel that there is an economic stake to the peace," Beblawi said.
But he added the Arab countries would have to set up an ambitious programme of integration going well beyond the dismantling of tariffs.

"They have to tackle the invisible barriers which prevent the free movement of people," he said. "Even more than the tariffs, they have to try to harmonise the legal system, the tax, the investment incentives and the property rights."
So far the only concrete step taken by the ministers of the eight countries involved was to assign a committee to prepare measures for the market. It is due to meet in September.
